source_text: Sed quidam discentes Pontici illius, supra magistrum sapere compuisi, concedunt Christo carnis veritatem, sine pracindicio tamen renueudae nativitatis. Habuerit, inquint, carnem dum omuino non natam. Pervenimus igitur de calcaria, quod dici solet, in carbonariam, a Marcione ad Apellen, qui, posteaquam a disciplina Marcionis in mulierem carne lapaus, dehinc in virginem Philumenen spiritu eversus est, solidum Christi corpus, sed sine nativitate suscepit ab eo praedicare. Et angelo quidem illi Philumenes eadem voce apostolus respondebit qua ipsum ilium iam tunc praecinebet, dicens, Etiamsi angelus de caelis aliter evangelizaverit vobis quam nos evangelizavimus, anathema sit. His vero, quae insuper argumentantur, nos resistemus. Confitentur vere corpus habuisse Christum. Unde materia, si non ex ea qualitate in qua videbatur? Unde corpus, si non caro corpus? Unde caro, si non nata? Quia nasci haberet ea futura quae nascitur, De sideribus, inquiunt, et de substantiis superioris mundi mutuatus est carnem. Et utique proponunt non esse mirandum corpus sine nativitate, cum et apud nos angelis licuerit nulla uteri opera in carnem processisse. Agnoscimus quidem ita relatum, sed tamen quale est ut alterius regulae fides ab ea fide quam impugnat instrumentum argumentationibus suis mutuetur? Quid illi cum Moyse qui deum Moysi reiecit? Si alius deus est, aliter sint res eius. Sed utantur haeretici omnes scripturis eius cuius utuntur etiam mundo. Erit illis hoc quoque testimonium iudicii, quod de exemplis ipsius blasphemias suas instruunt. Facile est veritati etiam nihil tale adversus cos praescribenti obtinere. Igitur qui carnem Christi ad exemplum proponunt angelorum, non natam dicentes, licat carnem, comparent velim et causas tam Christi quam et angelorum ob quas in carnem processerint. Nullus unquam angelus ideo descendit, ut crucifigeretur, ut mortem experiretur, ut a morte resuscitaretur. Si nunquam eiusmodi fuit causa angelorum corporanderum, habes causam cur non nascendo acceperint carnem. Non venerant mori, ideo nec nasci. At vero Christus mori missus nasci quoque necessario habuit, ut mori posset; non enim mori solet nisi quod nascitur. Mutuum debitum est nativitati cum mortalitate. Forma moriondi causa nascendi est. Si propter id quod moritur mortuus est Christus, id autem moritur quod et nascitur, consequens erat, immo praecedens, ut aeque nasceretur propter id quod nascitur, quia propter id ipsum mori habebat quod, quia nascitur, moritur. Non competebat non nasci pro quo mori competehat. Atquin tunc quoque inter angelos illos ipse dominus apparuit Abrahae sine nativitate, cum carne scilicet, pro eadem causae diversitate. Sed vos hoc non recipitis, non cum Christum recipientes qui iam tunc et adloqui et liberare et iudicare humanum genus ediscehat in earnis habitu non natae adhuc, quia nondum moriturae, nisi prius et nativitas eius et mortalitas annuntiarentur. Igitur probent angelos illos carnem de sideribus concepisse. Si non probant, quia nec scriptum est, nec Christi caro inde erit, cui angelorum accommodant exemplum. Constat angelos carnem non propriam portasse, utpote natura substantiae spiritalis, etsi corporis alicuius, sui tamen generis, in carnem autem humanam transfigurabiles ad tempus videri et congredi cum hominibus posse. Igitur cum relatum non sit unde sumpserint carnem, relinquitur intellectui nostro non dubitare hoc esse proprium angelicae potestatis, ex nulla materia corpus sibi sumere. Quanto magis, inquis, ex aliqua? Certum est. Sed nihil de hoc constat, quia scriptura non exhibet. Ceterum qui valent facere semetipsos quod natura non sunt, cur non valeant ex nulla substantia facere? Si fiunt quod non sunt, cur non ex eo fiant quod non est? Quod autem non est cum fit, ex nihilo est. Propterea nec requiritur nec ostenditur quid postea factum sit corporibus illorum. Quod de nihilo fuit, nihil factum est. Possunt nihil ipsum convertere in carnem qui semetipsos potuerunt convertere in carnem. Plus est naturam demutare quam facere materiam. Sed et si de materia necesse fuit angelos sumpsisse carnem, credibilius utique est de terrena materia quam de ullo genere caelestium substantiarum, cum adeo terrenae qualitatis extiterit ut terrenis pabulis pasta sit. Fuerit, sit nunc quoque siderea eodem modo terrenis pabulis pasta quando terrena non esset, quo terrena caelestibus pasta est quando caelestis non esset (legimus enim manna esui populo fuisse: Panem, inquit, angelorum edit homo), non tamen infringitur semel separata conditio dominicae carnis ex causa alterius dispositionis. Homo vere futurus usque ad mortem eam carnem oportebat indueret cuius est mors. Eam porro carnem, cuius est mors, nativitas antecedit.
orientation: Apelles once a follower of Marcion claims Christ had real flesh borrowed from starry things without birth like angels and Tertullian answers why birth was needed for death.
pass_a_gloss: But certain learners of that man of Pontus, compelled to be wise above their master, grant to Christ truth of flesh, yet without loss to birth that must be denied. Let him have had flesh, they say, provided in no way born. We have come therefore from lime pit, as it is commonly said, into coal pit, from Marcion to Apelles, who, after he fell in flesh into a woman away from the discipline of Marcion, then was overturned in spirit into the virgin Philumene, undertook to preach from him a solid body of Christ, but without birth. And to that angel of Philumene indeed the apostle will answer with the same voice with which he already then was foretelling that very man, saying, Even if an angel from heaven shall preach to you otherwise than we preached, let him be accursed. But to these things which moreover they argue, we will stand against. They confess that Christ truly had a body. Whence matter, if not from that quality in which it was seen. Whence body, if body is not flesh. Whence flesh, if not born. Because what is born had to be born. From starry things, they say, and from substances of the upper world he borrowed flesh. And assuredly they set forth that body without birth is not to be wondered at, since also among us it was allowed to angels with no work of womb to have come forth into flesh. We indeed acknowledge it so reported, but yet what kind of thing is it that faith of another rule should borrow from that faith which it attacks a tool for its own arguments. What has he to do with Moses who rejected the God of Moses. If his god is other, let his things be other. But let all heretics use the scriptures of him whose world also they use. This also will be for them a testimony of judgment, that from his examples they furnish their blasphemies. It is easy for truth to prevail even when prescribing nothing of this sort against them. Therefore those who set forth the flesh of Christ after the example of angels, saying it was not born, although flesh, I would wish them to compare also the causes both of Christ and of angels for which they came forth into flesh. No angel ever descended for this reason, that he might be crucified, that he might experience death, that he might be raised from death. If never was such the cause of angels taking body, you have the cause why they received flesh without birth. They had not come to die, therefore also not to be born. But Christ sent to die had of necessity also to be born, that he might be able to die. For nothing is accustomed to die except what is born. Birth has a mutual debt with mortality. The form of dying is the cause of birth. If Christ died on account of that which dies, but that dies which also is born, it was consequent, nay antecedent, that he should equally be born on account of that which is born, because on account of that very thing he had to die which, because it is born, dies. It was not fitting for him not to be born for whom it was fitting to die. But then also among those angels the Lord himself appeared to Abraham without birth, with flesh of course, for the same diversity of cause. But you do not receive this, not receiving Christ with it who already then was learning to address and to free and to judge the race of men in dress of flesh not yet born, because not yet to die, unless first both his birth and his mortality were announced. Therefore let them prove that those angels drew flesh from starry things. If they do not prove it, because neither is it written, neither will the flesh of Christ be from there, to which they fit the example of angels. It is agreed that angels bore flesh not their own, inasmuch as by nature of spiritual substance, although of some body, yet of its own kind, but able to be changed into flesh of men for a time so as to be seen and to meet with men. Therefore since it is not reported whence they took flesh, it is left to our understanding not to doubt that this is proper to angelic power, to take to itself a body from no matter. How much more, you say, from some matter. It is certain. But nothing about this is settled, because scripture does not exhibit it. Moreover those who are able to make themselves what by nature they are not, why should they not be able to make from no substance. If they become what they are not, why should they not become from what is not. But what is not, when it comes to be, is from nothing. Therefore neither is it inquired nor is it shown what afterwards became of those bodies of theirs. What was from nothing became nothing. They who were able to turn themselves into flesh are able to turn nothing itself into flesh. It is more to change nature than to make matter. But even if it was necessary for angels to have taken flesh from matter, it is more credible assuredly from earthly matter than from any kind of heavenly substances, since it proved of so earthly quality that it was fed with earthly foods. Let it have been, let it be even now starry in the same way fed with earthly foods when it would not be earthly, in the same way in which earthly flesh was fed with heavenly foods when it would not be heavenly, for we read that manna was for food to the people, Bread of angels man ate, yet the once separated condition of the flesh of the Lord is not broken by reason of another ordering. Truly to be man even unto death he had to put on that flesh whose property death is. Moreover that flesh whose property death is, birth goes before.

pass_b_english: But some disciples of that Pontic master, driven to seem wiser than their teacher, grant Christ the truth of the flesh, yet without giving up their denial of his birth. He had flesh, they say, but wholly unborn. So we have come, as the saying goes, from lime pit into coal pit, from Marcion to Apelles. After falling in the flesh into a woman and breaking with the school of Marcion, Apelles was then turned in spirit toward the virgin Philumene, and he took up preaching from her the solid body of Christ, but without birth. To that angel of Philumene the apostle will answer with the same voice with which he already then foretold him, saying, "Even if an angel from heaven proclaims to you a different gospel than the one we proclaimed to you, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8). Against their further arguments we will make our stand.

They admit that Christ truly had a body. Then where does its matter come from, if not from the condition in which it appeared? Where does a body come from, if a body is not flesh? Where does flesh come from, if it was not born? For whatever is destined to be born must be born. From the stars, they say, and from substances of the upper world he borrowed flesh. And they insist there is nothing strange in a body without birth, since even among us angels were able to proceed into flesh with no work of a womb. We grant that Scripture reports this. But how can the faith of one rule borrow the weapon for its own arguments from the very faith it attacks? What has he to do with Moses, when he has rejected the God of Moses? If his god is another, let that god's realities be otherwise. Still, let all heretics use the Scriptures of the one whose world they also use. This too will stand as testimony of judgment against them, that they build their blasphemies out of his own examples. It is easy for the truth to win, even when it enters no such plea against them.

So let those who cite the angels as the pattern for the flesh of Christ, calling it unborn though flesh, compare the reasons why Christ and why the angels proceeded into flesh. No angel ever came down to be crucified, to undergo death, to be raised from death. If the angels' taking of bodies never had such a cause, you have the reason why they received flesh without birth. They had not come to die, and so they had not come to be born. But Christ, sent to die, had also to be born of necessity, so that he could die. For commonly only what is born dies. Birth has a mutual debt with mortality. The shape of dying is the cause of birth. If Christ died on account of what dies, and what dies is what is also born, it followed, indeed it came first, that he should equally be born on account of what is born, because he had to die on account of the very thing which dies because it is born. It did not fit him to remain unborn for the sake of that for which it fitted him to die. Yet even then, among those angels, the Lord himself appeared to Abraham without birth, with flesh of course, for the same difference of cause. But you do not accept this, since you do not accept Christ, who even then was learning to address and free and judge the human race in the garb of flesh not yet born, because not yet to die, until his birth and his mortality were first announced. Let them then prove that those angels drew flesh from the stars. If they cannot prove it, because it is not written, then the flesh of Christ will not come from there either, though they fit the angels to him as an example.

It is agreed that the angels bore flesh not their own, since by nature they are of spiritual substance, though of some body of their own kind, yet able for a time to appear transformed into flesh and to meet with men. Since Scripture does not report where they took flesh from, our understanding is left with no doubt that this belongs to angelic power, to take to itself a body from no matter. How much more readily, you ask, from some matter? That is certain. But nothing is settled on this point, because Scripture shows nothing. Moreover, if they can make themselves what by nature they are not, why can they not make from no substance? If they become what they are not, why should they not become from what is not? And what is not, when it comes to be, is from nothing. So Scripture neither asks nor shows what afterward became of those bodies. What was from nothing became nothing. Those who could turn themselves into flesh can turn nothing itself into flesh. It is greater to change nature than to make matter. But even if the angels had to take flesh from matter, it is surely more credible that they took it from earthly matter than from any kind of heavenly substances, since their flesh proved of so earthly a quality that it fed on earthly foods. Suppose it was starry, and even now starry, fed in the same way on earthly foods though it would not be earthly, just as what was earthly fed on heavenly foods though it would not be heavenly, for we read that manna was given to the people for food: "Man ate the bread of angels" (Psalm 78:25). Still, the condition of the Lord's flesh, once set apart, is not broken by the cause of a different arrangement. Since he was to be truly man even unto death, he had to put on that flesh whose mark is death. And birth comes before that flesh whose mark is death.
notes: Possible OCR damage in source spellings compuisi for compulsi and pracindicio for praeiudicio and renueudae for renuendae and omuino for omnino, gloss follows probable sense
Clause Quia nasci haberet ea futura quae nascitur is obscure, gloss renders words as they stand without supplying missing text

problems.quote: Apelles was then overturned in spirit by the virgin Philumene
problems.source_quote: dehinc in virginem Philumenen spiritu eversus est
problems.why: In + accusative makes Philumene the one he fell toward, parallel to the woman, not the agent who overthrew him.
problems.fix: Apelles was then turned in spirit toward the virgin Philumene
problems.ruling: "in virginem Philumenen" is in+accusative: Apelles was overthrown in spirit toward/into Philumene, parallel to "in mulierem"; "by" makes her the agent.

problems.quote: in the garb of flesh not yet born, because his birth and his mortality had not yet been announced
problems.source_quote: in carnis habitu non natae adhuc, quia nondum moriturae, nisi prius et nativitas eius et mortalitas annuntiarentur
problems.why: Drops that the flesh was not yet to die, and turns “unless first announced” into a bare because.
problems.fix: in the garb of flesh not yet born, because not yet to die, until his birth and his mortality were first announced
problems.ruling: "quia nondum moriturae" (not yet to die) is dropped, and "nisi prius ... annuntiarentur" (unless first announced) becomes a bare "because", which weakens the argument.

fixed: agency: fixed — 'in virginem Philumenen' is accusative of direction parallel to 'in mulierem', not agent; changed to turned toward.
